module.title: Human Oversight / Human in the Loop

working in pharma, quality assurance,
IT, or validation, you already know that
EU GMP Annex 22 is completely shifting
how we handle artificial intelligence in
our critical systems. But today, we're
going to do something a bit different.
We're taking the really dry regulatory
compliance mandates of module 10,
specifically the rules around human
oversight and human in the loop, and
transforming them into a highly
practical operational playbook. We are
going to break down exactly how you can
engineer meaningful oversight that
inspectors will actually respect. Okay,
let's dive into our road map for this
explainer. We'll start with why human
oversight matters, then look at the
three oversight tiers, the automation
bias trap, designing meaningful review
workflows, and finally, proving
compliance to inspectors. Section one,
why human oversight matters. To get this
right, we really have to understand the
core philosophy behind the regulation.
Bringing AI into GXP environments
doesn't replace human judgment.
Actually, it paradoxically amplifies the
absolute need for it. So, I want to pose
a direct question, especially to the QA
and validation folks tuning in right
now. Does AI autonomy truly exist in
critical GXP applications? I mean, when
patient risk is on the line and
regulatory scrutiny is peaking, can we
ever just let the machine run the whole
show? Well, the short answer from an
Annex 22 perspective is absolutely not.
No way.
The absolute biggest trap an
organization can fall into is what
inspectors call perfunctory oversight.
This is nominal oversight. It's when a
highly trained professional simply
stares at a screen and clicks approve on
whatever the AI suggests. Sure, it gives
management this false sense of comfort,
but under Annex 22, it is a direct
one-way ticket to regulatory failure. If
your reviewers aren't genuinely engaged,
you don't actually have oversight. It's
just an illusion.
Moving on to section two, the three
oversight tiers. Let's break down the
strict rules governing exactly how
humans and AI are supposed to interact.
And this breakdown brilliantly
illustrates what Annex 22 mandates. We
have three oversight tiers, perfectly
matched to patient risk. Up at the top,
there's HILL, or human in the loop.
That's for high-risk GMP decisions, like
batch release. Below that is HOTL, human
on the loop. This is for moderate-risk
tasks, like process parameter
optimization. The AI acts, but a human
supervises and can intervene. And at the
very bottom, we have HOOL, human out of

like inventory rebalancing. Let me be
incredibly clear here. HOOL is rarely,

applications.
Let's really focus in on the gold
standard for high criticality, which is
human in the loop.
Operationally speaking, this means your
reviewers literally must evaluate every
single AI output before any action is
taken. It's the default, it's the
strongest control available. Now, yes,
obviously, this comes with a slower
throughput. It's a real operational
cost. But the expectation here isn't
just passive observation. Reviewers must
actively challenge the AI. They need
application-specific training, so they
know the AI's limitations, they can spot
its biases, and they recognize those
weird edge cases that warrant much
deeper analysis.
Section three, the automation bias trap.
You know, maintaining that active
challenge we just talked about is
incredibly difficult over time. And that
leads us to one of the most dangerous
operational hazards you're going to
face. We really need to talk about
automation bias. It's a well-documented
cognitive tendency. It's just human
nature to over-trust automated systems,
especially when those systems are right
most of the time. You can have the most
diligent, highly qualified subject
matter experts in your lab, but if they
are constantly handed AI suggestions,
they will slowly default to just
confirming those outputs. It's a silent,
creeping decay of oversight.
To show you what this actually looks
like in the real world, consider this
anonymized case study.
We're looking at a deviation triage AI
that was deployed human in the loop
oversight. In month one, reviewers were
actively overriding the AI's severity
classifications about 12% of the time.
But by month three, internal audits
started showing a gradual decline in
disagreements. And by month six, the
override rate plummeted to a mere 1.5%.
Now, what's really interesting here is
the sheer magnitude of that drop. Going
from 12% to 1.5%
doesn't happen because the AI suddenly
got 10 times smarter. It happens because
the humans simply stop thinking
critically. And the real-world impact
was severe.
Managers doing retrospective reviews
found that several deviations actually
required severity reclassification. One
of them even warranted CAPA escalation.
So, if your override rate is trending
towards zero, that is a massive red
flag. Section four, designing meaningful
review workflows. Let's pivot away from
the psychological trap and get into the
operational blueprint. The solution to
all of this lies entirely in your
workflow design. Look at the difference
between these two approaches. With
nominal confirmation, the reviewer sees
the AI suggestion immediately and
basically just clicks approve. That
right there breeds automation bias. But
then we have the independent first
pattern. This is where the reviewer
evaluates the data and makes their own
classification before they are ever
allowed to see the AI suggestion. If the
two match, great. If they disagree, it
triggers a documented adjudication
process. This independent first pattern
literally forces genuine engagement and
preserves independent judgment.
For the IT and system owners listening,
building robust escalation mechanisms is
another critical design pattern. Step
one, the AI handles routine cases, but
flags edge cases based on specific
confidence thresholds. Step two, the
system automatically escalates these to
a human review queue, giving the
reviewer full context. And that means
showing not just the data, but exactly
why the AI lacked confidence. Step
three, a senior reviewer determines the
disposition and crucially documents the
rationale contemporaneously. This
escalation path has to align seamlessly
with your existing deviation and
complaint processes.
Finally, section five, proving
compliance to inspectors because an
unproven system is a non-compliant
system. Let's look at our final
takeaways directly through the
inspector's lens.

exactly what metrics an inspector will
